q: Sharks are what kind of animal?
why: Sharks breathe underwater with gills, like other fish. Whales and dolphins breathe air, so they are mammals.
hint: Think about how a shark breathes underwater.

q: Put the butterfly's life in order, from the very start.
why: A butterfly changes shape completely. It hatches as a caterpillar and grows before it turns into a butterfly.
hint: A butterfly begins very small.

q: What is the Sun?
why: The Sun is a star, a giant ball of hot glowing gas. Planets and moons only shine by reflecting light.
hint: It makes its own light.

q: Dinosaurs like T. rex lived at the same time as people.
why: Big dinosaurs like T. rex died out about 66 million years ago, long before the first people.
hint: Think about how old fossils are.

q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
why: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood to the gills and one pumps blood to the body.
hint: It is more than you have, but fewer than five.

q: What job do roots do for a plant?
opts: Make the seeds for new plants
why: Roots drink water from the soil and hold the plant in place. Flowers make seeds and attract bees.
hint: Roots grow underground.

q: Which of these is a PULL?
why: A pull moves something toward you. Kicking and hitting push things away.
hint: A pull brings something closer to you.

q: Put these animals in order from smallest to biggest.
why: Each animal is bigger than the one before. A blue whale is longer than two school buses.
hint: Think about how much space each one takes up.

q: The Moon makes its own light.
why: The Moon shines because it bounces back light from the Sun. Only stars make their own light.
hint: What lights up the Moon at night?

q: Put the life of a plant in order, from the start.
why: A seed sprouts roots and a stem, grows into a small plant, and then makes flowers.
hint: Everything begins as a seed.

q: Which part of a shark's body sweeps side to side to push it forward?
why: The tail fin swishes back and forth and drives the shark through the water. Gills are for breathing.
hint: Think about what pushes a swimming fish forward.

q: Put the water cycle in order, starting with the Sun heating the sea.
why: Heat turns sea water into invisible vapor. High up it cools into cloud drops, and rain returns the water.
hint: What happens first: warming or cooling?

q: Triceratops was a herbivore. What did it eat?
why: Herbivores eat only plants. Tyrannosaurus rex was a carnivore and ate meat.
hint: Herb- sounds like herbs and plants.

q: Sound is made when something vibrates, or wiggles back and forth very fast.
why: Pluck a rubber band and you can see it wiggle. Those fast wiggles make the sound you hear.
hint: Touch your throat while you hum.

q: How many legs does an insect have?
why: All insects have six legs. Spiders have eight legs, so they are not insects.
hint: Count the legs on an ant.

q: Why is it dark at night?
opts: Our side of Earth turns from the Sun
The Sun gets switched off until morning
The Moon moves in front of the Sun
why: Earth spins like a top. When your part turns away from the Sun, it is night.
hint: Earth keeps turning around.

q: Put these planets in order, starting closest to the Sun.
why: A memory trick: My Very Eager Mother. Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars come first.
hint: Mercury is the closest.

q: Friction slows down a baseball that rolls across the grass.
why: Friction is rubbing between two things. The grass rubs the ball and slows it until it stops.
hint: Why does a rolling ball stop?

q: Which body part pumps blood around your body?
why: The heart is a strong muscle that pumps blood. Lungs bring in air and the stomach breaks down food.
hint: Put your hand on your chest.

q: Put a frog's life in order, from the start.
why: Tadpoles breathe with gills, then grow legs and lungs and change into frogs.
hint: Tadpoles live in water.

q: A shark's skin feels like sandpaper. What covers it?
why: Shark skin is covered with tiny scales shaped like teeth. They help water flow smoothly past the shark.
hint: Think rough, not soft.

q: What is a fossil?
opts: A trace of ancient life in rock
A rock made from cooled lava
A seashell that washed up this year
A plant that grows deep in caves
why: Fossils are bones, shells, footprints or other traces of living things preserved in rock for a very long time.
hint: Fossils show us living things from long ago.

q: Put these giant planets in order, starting closest to the Sun.
why: The four giant planets lie beyond Mars and the asteroid belt. Jupiter is nearest the Sun and Neptune is farthest.
hint: They all come after Mars.

q: A seesaw is an example of which simple machine?
why: A lever is a bar that turns around a point called a fulcrum. A seesaw turns on its middle.
hint: It tips back and forth on a middle point.

q: In a fair test, you change only one thing at a time.
why: If you change two things, you cannot tell which one caused the result.
hint: Think about testing two paper airplanes.

q: Water boils at about how many degrees Celsius at sea level?
why: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius and freezes at 0. That is 212 and 32 degrees Fahrenheit.
hint: It is a nice round number.

q: Coral reefs are built by tiny animals. What are they called?
why: Coral polyps build hard skeletons around themselves. Over a very long time, many polyps build a reef.
hint: They are tiny and stay in one place.

q: Sharks have hard bones inside their bodies.
why: A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage, the bendy stuff in your ears and nose, not bone.
hint: Feel the end of your nose.

q: Why does the Moon seem to change shape each night?
opts: We see changing amounts of its lit half
Earth's shadow covers different parts of it
Clouds in space cover different parts of it
It melts and regrows every single month
why: The Moon is always half lit by the Sun. As it orbits Earth, we see more or less of that lit half.
hint: The Moon itself never changes shape.

q: Put this ocean food chain in order, starting with the energy source.
why: Seaweed uses sunlight to make food, small fish eat the seaweed, and sharks eat the fish.
hint: Where does all the energy start?

q: A shark loses a tooth while biting. What happens next?
opts: A new tooth grows back in one day
A spare tooth moves up to replace it
Nothing happens; sharks keep all teeth
It stops eating until the tooth regrows
why: Sharks have rows of spare teeth behind the front ones. They move forward like a conveyor belt.
hint: Sharks have many rows of teeth.

q: Long lines of fossil dinosaur footprints can show scientists what?
opts: What it ate for its last lunch
What sounds it made when it roared
How it moved and how big it was
What color its skin and eyes were
why: Footprints are trace fossils. Their spacing shows how fast the dinosaur walked, and their size hints at its body.
hint: Footprints record movement, not color.

q: Put Earth's layers in order, starting at the outside.
why: We live on the thin crust. Below it are the thick mantle, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core.
hint: Go from where we live down to the center.

q: A hit baseball flies, slows down, then falls. Which forces act on it in the air?
opts: Gravity and a lasting push from the bat
why: Gravity pulls the ball down and air pushes against it. The bat's push ends the moment they separate.
hint: Think about what pushes back as the ball moves.

q: On the Moon, a hammer and a feather dropped together land at the same time.
why: The Moon has no air to slow the feather. Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott showed this in 1971.
hint: What would slow the feather on Earth?

q: How many chambers (rooms) does a human heart have?
why: Two small chambers on top take in blood. Two strong chambers on the bottom pump it out.
hint: Two on top, two on the bottom.

q: What mainly causes ocean tides?
opts: The pull of the Moon's gravity
Rivers pushing water out to sea
why: The Moon's gravity tugs on the ocean and makes the water bulge. The Sun adds a smaller pull.
hint: Something far away in space is pulling.

q: Put the ocean zones in order, from the surface down.
why: Light fades with depth. Below about 1,000 meters it is completely dark, and the water is near freezing.
hint: The sunlit zone is the one near the top.

q: Sound travels faster through water than through air.
why: Water's tiny particles are packed closer together, so sound passes along them faster. That helps whales call far away.
hint: Think about how whales communicate.

q: You see wet footprints by a pool and say, "Someone just swam here." What is that?
why: An observation is what you sense, like wet footprints. An inference is a smart explanation based on it.
hint: Is it what you saw, or what you figured out?

q: A nurse shark can rest on the sea floor without swimming. How does it still breathe?
opts: It pumps water over its gills
It uses a blowhole like a whale
It gulps air at the surface
why: Some sharks can use their mouth and throat to pump water over the gills. Others must swim to keep water flowing.
hint: Gills need a steady flow of water.

q: Which living animals are the closest relatives of Tyrannosaurus rex?
why: Fossils show many meat-eating dinosaurs had feathers and wishbones. Birds are their living descendants.
hint: Think feathers and wishbones.

q: Put these planets in order from smallest to largest.
why: Mercury and Mars are small and rocky. Earth is bigger, and Neptune and Jupiter are giant planets.
hint: Rocky planets are smaller than giant planets.

q: A bat hits a baseball and the ball speeds up. Where did its extra motion energy come from?
why: Energy passes from the moving bat to the ball. That is why a faster swing sends the ball farther.
hint: What was moving before they touched?

q: Earth has seasons because it moves closer to and farther from the Sun.
why: Seasons come from Earth's tilt. When your part of Earth leans toward the Sun, it gets stronger sunlight and summer.
hint: Think about Earth's tilt.

q: A pitch travels 18 meters in half a second. How many meters does it travel each second at that speed?
why: Half a second goes into one second twice, so double the distance: 18 times 2 is 36 meters.
hint: Double the distance.

q: Why does ocean water taste salty?
opts: Fish give off salt as they swim
Waves mix in salt from the sea air
Rivers wash rock salts into the sea
The Sun bakes salt into the sea water
why: Water evaporates from the sea but the salts stay behind, so over millions of years the ocean got salty.
hint: Salt comes from rocks.

q: Put these in order from smallest to largest.
why: Cells join to make tissues, tissues make organs, and organs work together in systems of the body.
hint: Start with the tiniest building block.

q: Sound can travel through outer space just like it travels through air.
why: Space is almost empty, so there is nothing to carry the vibrations. In space, no one can hear a rocket roar.
hint: Sound needs something to wiggle.

q: You test whether warm water melts ice faster. Which should stay the SAME in every cup?
opts: The size of the ice cubes
The time it takes to melt
why: The thing you change is the water temperature. The ice size must be the same so the test is fair.
hint: Keep everything the same except one thing.

q: Sharks have jelly-filled pores on their snouts called ampullae of Lorenzini. What do they sense?
opts: Faint light from deep in the water
How salty the water around it is
Sound waves coming from far away
why: Living animals give off a faint electric field. Sharks can feel it, even when the prey is hidden in sand.
hint: It is a sense humans do not have.

q: Similar dinosaur fossils are found on continents now far apart. What helps explain this?
opts: Dinosaurs swam across oceans each year
Wind blew bones across the sea
Those lands were once joined together
Fossils form in the same way everywhere
why: Continents slowly drift on moving plates. Long ago many lands were connected, so animals could walk between them.
hint: Think about plate tectonics.

q: Put the Moon's phases in order, starting at new moon.
why: The lit part grows to a full moon in about two weeks, then shrinks through last quarter back to new.
hint: The lit part grows first, then shrinks.

q: A curveball curves in flight. What makes it curve?
opts: Gravity pulls harder on spinning balls
Spin changes air pressure around it
One side of the ball gets much heavier
Strong wind always pushes it sideways
why: Spin drags air around the ball, so the pressure is unequal on its sides. The higher pressure pushes it sideways.
hint: Think about the ball's spin.

q: Mercury's year (one trip around the Sun) is longer than Earth's year.
why: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, so it travels a shorter path much faster. Its year is only about 88 days.
hint: Closer planets orbit faster.

q: Sound travels about 340 meters each second in air. You hear thunder 3 seconds after you see lightning. About how many meters away was the lightning?
why: You see lightning almost instantly, so the delay is the sound's trip. 340 times 3 equals 1,020 meters.
hint: Multiply the speed by the time.

q: The deeper you dive in the ocean, the more the water presses on you. Why?
opts: The water gets saltier and sticky
More water is stacked above you
why: The water above you has weight, and the deeper you go, the more of it you carry. Divers feel pressure in their ears.
hint: Think about a pile of books on you.

q: Put the life of a star like our Sun in order.
why: A star forms from a cloud, shines steadily for billions of years, swells into a red giant, then shrinks to a white dwarf.
hint: Stars are born in clouds.

q: Salt water freezes at a lower temperature than fresh water.
why: Salt gets in the way of ice crystals forming. The ocean must be colder than 0 degrees Celsius to freeze.
hint: Why do we put salt on icy roads?

q: A student grows one bean plant in sun and one in the dark and decides light helps beans grow. What would make the test more trustworthy?
opts: Test several plants in each place
Use a bigger pot for the sunny plant
why: One plant could grow badly by chance. Using many plants in each place makes the pattern easier to trust.
hint: One try could be luck.

q: A whale swims north. Which way is the opposite direction?
why: North and south are opposites, and so are east and west.
hint: Picture a compass: what is across from north?

q: Which of these is a NEED, not just a want?
why: Needs are things people must have to live, like food, water and shelter. Wants are nice extras.
hint: What do you need to stay alive?

q: Put these places in order from smallest to biggest.
why: Maps zoom out like this: a room sits inside a house, a house in a city, and a city in a country.
hint: Each place fits inside the next one.

q: Penguins live at the North Pole.
why: Penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere, like Antarctica. Polar bears are the ones that live near the North Pole.
hint: Which pole is in the far south?

q: Most maps used in the United States show how many continents?
why: The seven continents are Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America.
hint: Count them on a globe.

q: The Great Pyramids were built long ago in the desert of which continent?
why: The Great Pyramids stand in Egypt, in northern Africa. Ancient Egyptians built them as tombs for their kings.
hint: Egypt is next to the Sahara.

q: Giant tortoises live on the Galápagos Islands. Which ocean are the islands in?
why: The Galápagos Islands sit in the Pacific Ocean, off the west coast of South America.
hint: They are west of South America.

q: Put the compass directions in order going clockwise, starting at north.
why: Clockwise is the way clock hands move. A trick: Never Eat Soggy Waffles.
hint: Think of a clock face.

q: In Spanish, the word "tiburón" means which animal?
why: Tiburón is Spanish for shark. Ballena means whale and tortuga means turtle.
hint: Think of a fin sticking out of the water.

q: Put these steps in order for buying a baseball glove.
why: You need to earn money first, then save it until you have enough, and then spend it.
hint: You cannot spend money you do not have.

q: Emperor penguins raise their chicks on which icy continent?
why: Antarctica is a cold continent at the bottom of the world, where emperor penguins gather to raise chicks.
hint: It is at the South Pole.

q: What does a compass rose on a map show?
why: The compass rose points out north, south, east and west so you can read the map.
hint: It looks like a star with letters.

q: Put these four oceans in order from largest to smallest.
why: The Pacific covers about a third of Earth. The Arctic Ocean is the smallest of these four.
hint: The Pacific is biggest, the Arctic coldest and smallest.

q: The country Ecuador is named after a line around the middle of Earth. What is it?
why: Ecuador is the Spanish word for equator. The country sits right on that line.
hint: Spanish: ecuador. English: ...

q: The Hawaiian Islands are in the Pacific Ocean.
why: Hawaii is a chain of islands in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, far from any continent.
hint: Think of surfing and volcanoes.

q: On a map legend, 1 tree symbol means 10 real trees. A forest shows 3 tree symbols. How many real trees are there?
why: A map legend explains what symbols mean. Three symbols times 10 trees each is 30 trees.
hint: Count by tens.

q: Which famous tower is in Paris, France?
why: The Eiffel Tower stands in Paris. The Leaning Tower is in Pisa, Italy, and Big Ben is in London.
hint: It is made of iron lattice.

q: The Bahamas are famous for being made of many what?
why: The Bahamas are a chain of hundreds of islands in the Atlantic Ocean, with warm, clear water around them.
hint: Picture palm trees and beaches with turquoise water.

q: All deserts are hot and sandy.
why: A desert is a place with very little rain. Antarctica is a cold desert covered in ice.
hint: Deserts are about rain, not heat.

q: Put the steps of running a lemonade stand in order.
why: You pay for supplies first (your cost), then make and sell the product, and finally count what you earned.
hint: You make it before you sell it.

q: The Galápagos Islands are part of which country?
why: The Galápagos belong to Ecuador, even though they are about 1,000 kilometers out in the Pacific Ocean.
hint: They sit in the Pacific, west of South America.

q: What does a map scale help you find out?
opts: Which way is north on the map
The names of all the countries
why: A scale like 1 cm = 10 km turns map distances into real distances. A compass rose shows direction.
hint: It looks like a little ruler.

q: Put these buildings in order from oldest to newest.
why: The Great Pyramid is about 4,500 years old. The Eiffel Tower was finished in 1889, so it is the newest.
hint: Ancient builders came before iron towers.

q: Profit is the money you have left after you...
why: A lemonade stand earns $12 and spent $5 on supplies, so the profit is $7. Profit is earnings minus costs.
hint: Earnings minus what you spent.

q: The Equator is a line that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole.
why: The Equator runs around the middle of Earth, east to west. Lines from pole to pole are called meridians.
hint: Does it circle the middle or go up and down?

q: You buy a used baseball glove for $12 and sell it for $20. How many dollars of profit do you make?
why: Profit is what you sell for minus what you paid: 20 minus 12 equals 8.
hint: Subtract the cost from the price.

q: The Great Barrier Reef, a huge coral reef, is off the coast of which continent?
why: The Great Barrier Reef lies off the northeast coast of Australia in the Coral Sea.
hint: It is also called the Land Down Under.

q: Put these cities in order from north to south.
why: This is the Pacific coast of North America. Each city is a little farther south than the one before.
hint: Canada is the farthest north.

q: The Hawaiian Islands were built by volcanoes rising from the sea floor.
why: Lava built up from the ocean floor over millions of years until it poked above the surface as islands.
hint: Think of Kilauea.

q: Put these cities in order from west to east.
why: Honolulu is out in the Pacific Ocean. Heading east you reach the Pacific coast, the Rocky Mountains and the Atlantic coast.
hint: Start in the Pacific Ocean.

q: The Equator divides Earth into which two halves?
opts: A land half and a water half
The day side and the night side
why: The Equator splits Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. The Prime Meridian splits east from west.
hint: The Equator is the halfway line between the poles.

q: Mount Rainier, a snowy volcano near Seattle, belongs to which mountain range?
why: The Cascades run from Canada through Washington and Oregon. The Rockies are farther east, and the Appalachians are on the other side of the country.
hint: This range is in the Pacific Northwest.

q: Put these climate zones in order, from the Equator toward the North Pole.
why: It gets cooler as you travel away from the Equator. Tropical is warmest, temperate is in between, and polar is coldest.
hint: Start where it is warmest.

q: Only 5 rare baseball cards are for sale, but 50 kids want one. What will probably happen to the price?
why: When a lot of people want something that is in short supply, sellers can ask for more money.
hint: Think about how many cards there are compared to kids.

q: The Equator passes through the Galápagos Islands.
why: The line crosses Isabela Island, so the Galápagos lie in both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
hint: Think about which country the islands belong to.

q: Florida is a peninsula. What does that mean?
opts: It has no coast or beaches
It stands on top of a mountain
Water touches it on three sides
Water surrounds it on every side
why: A peninsula is land that sticks out into the water. An island is surrounded by water on every side.
hint: Look at Florida on a map.

q: A map scale says 1 cm = 5 km. A tagged shark's path is 4 cm long on the map. How many kilometers did it swim?
why: Every centimeter on the map stands for 5 real kilometers. Four centimeters is 4 times 5.
hint: Multiply the map distance by the scale.

q: Long ago, sailors steered at night by one star in the northern sky that hardly seems to move. What is it called?
why: The North Star, Polaris, sits almost straight above the North Pole. Sailors knew it showed them north.
hint: Its name tells you which way it points.

q: Put these steps in order for how bread reaches a store.
why: Goods pass through many workers before you buy them. Each step needs the one before it.
hint: The wheat has to exist first.

q: A bank pays you a little extra money for keeping your savings there. What is that extra money called?
why: Interest is a small reward for letting the bank use your savings. The longer you save, the more it can grow.
hint: It is money that your money earns.

q: Which imaginary lines run east to west and tell you how far north or south a place is?
why: Latitude lines are like the rungs of a ladder. Longitude lines run from pole to pole.
hint: Picture the rungs of a ladder.

q: A baseball game in New York starts at 7:00 PM New York time. New York is 3 hours ahead of Los Angeles. What hour is it in Los Angeles then?
why: Places farther west have earlier clock times, because the Sun reaches the east first. Subtract 3 hours from 7.
hint: Which way do you go on the clock?

q: You have $10 and choose a baseball cap instead of a book. What is the book called in this choice?
why: Opportunity cost is the next best thing you give up when you choose. It is not the money, but the lost choice.
hint: It is what you gave up.

q: Put these cities in order, from nearest to farthest from the Equator.
why: Quito is almost on the Equator. Each city after it is farther north.
hint: One of them sits almost on the Equator.

q: If a storm destroys many orange crops, orange juice will probably cost more.
why: Fewer oranges means a smaller supply. When something becomes scarce, sellers can charge a higher price.
hint: Think about supply and price.

q: Why are river deltas, where a river reaches the sea, often good for farming?
opts: The land is high and rocky
why: Rivers carry bits of soil downstream. At the delta the water slows and drops it, making soil full of nutrients.
hint: Think about what a slow river drops.

q: The Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans all touch a cold ocean that circles Antarctica. What is it called?
why: The Southern Ocean wraps around Antarctica. The Arctic Ocean is near the North Pole.
hint: Its name tells you its direction.

q: The Prime Meridian is the line of 0 degrees longitude.
why: Longitude is measured east and west from the Prime Meridian. It passes through Greenwich, near London.
hint: It is the starting line for longitude.

q: Why are the polar regions cold all year?
opts: They are the closest places to the Sun
Cold winds from space cool them
Sunlight arrives at a low slant
The Sun never shines on them at all
why: Near the poles the Sun's rays hit at a low angle and cover a larger area, so each spot gets less heat.
hint: Think about a flashlight shining at a slant.

q: Ancient Egyptian builders used ramps and levers to help move heavy stones. A ramp is which simple machine?
why: An inclined plane is a slanted surface. It lets you raise a load with less push over a longer distance.
hint: It is a slanted surface.

q: Quito, Ecuador, sits almost on the Equator but has cool, spring-like weather. Why?
opts: It sits farther from the Sun
It sits high in the Andes
Snow falls on it all year long
why: Air gets colder as elevation rises. Quito is about 2,850 meters up, so the Equator's heat is cooled by the altitude.
hint: Think about how it feels at the top of a tall mountain.

q: Each time zone is about 15 degrees of longitude wide. Earth is 360 degrees around. About how many time zones fit around the whole Earth?
why: 360 divided by 15 is 24. That matches the 24 hours in a day, because Earth turns once a day.
hint: Divide 360 by 15.

q: Seattle gets lots of rain, but the land just east of the Cascade Mountains is dry. Why?
opts: Mountains squeeze rain from the air
The ocean is much colder east of them
Rain only ever falls near the coast
Dry winds blow in from the Atlantic
why: Moist Pacific air rises up the mountains, cools and drops rain. The air that descends the other side is dry.
hint: What happens to air as it rises over a mountain?

q: Put these ways of finding direction at sea in order, from oldest to newest.
why: Sailors used stars first. Then they added the compass, and the sextant measured star angles. GPS satellites came last.
hint: Satellites are the newest invention here.

q: A place at 30 degrees South latitude and 120 degrees West longitude is in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres.
why: South latitude means south of the Equator. West longitude means west of the Prime Meridian.
hint: Read the directions in each number.

q: Why did people invent money instead of only trading goods (barter)?
opts: Goods were always too heavy to carry
Only rich people were allowed to trade
Both must want what the other has
why: If you have fish and want wheat, the wheat seller must also want fish. Money works for everyone.
hint: Think about finding someone who wants your fish.

q: Why do islands far from any continent, like the Galápagos, often have animals found nowhere else?
opts: Islands have no predators or diseases
why: Few animals reach distant islands. Those that do live apart from their relatives and slowly change.
hint: Think about being cut off from the mainland.

q: Put these US time zones in order, from where the Sun rises first to where it rises last.
why: Earth turns from west to east, so the Sun reaches the east first. Noon comes to Eastern first and Pacific last.
hint: The Sun rises in the east.

q: Antarctic scientists study air bubbles trapped in very old ice. What can the bubbles tell them?
opts: What the air was like long ago
Which animals once lived on the ice
How deep the ocean is below it
why: Falling snow squeezes air into ice layers. Deeper layers hold older air, like pages in a very old book.
hint: Older ice holds older air.

q: A bakery raises the price of its cookies and fewer people buy them. Which idea does this show?
opts: Profit is always the same as price
Demand often falls when prices rise
why: When something costs more, fewer people want to buy it at that price. That is how demand usually works.
hint: Think about how shoppers react to a higher price.
